Ukraine said it attacked a major oil refinery in Russia’s Urals region as Kyiv’s campaign against energy infrastructure ratchets up pressure on Moscow’s oil exports and fuel production.

Long-range weapons hit Lukoil PJSC’s Perm refinery overnight, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Friday in a statement on Telegram, providing no further details.

The 260,000-barrel-a-day plant, located about 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) east of Moscow, was last attacked in late July. Ukraine has stepped up strikes against Russian energy assets in recent weeks, hitting refineries as well as port infrastructure on the Black Sea. The assaults have cut Russia’s oil exports to the lowest since April, while refinery runs have continued to fall.

Broad-based commodity gains gather momentum as weather risks, geopolitical disruption, tight supply and US fiscal concerns drive strength across energy, metals and agriculture. https://t.co/YNkKoPYtvk via @saxobank

#Commodities
Weather, war, fiscal debt concerns, and a softer dollar all supporting broad-based commodity gains this week, with the BCOM TR index rising around 3%, lifting its YTD return to 30%. All sectors except industrial metals traded higher, led by soft commodities with gains of around 5%, followed by precious metals and energy, also near 5%, while grains trailed with a roughly 3% advance. At the individual commodity level, platinum, silver, crude oil, diesel, sugar and cocoa all recorded gains of more than 5%, highlighting the increasingly broad nature of the current rally.
#CrudeOil: Brent rose to its highest level in almost four weeks near USD 95 after President Trump threatened Iran with economic warfare, before paring the advance to trade near USD 93.5, with WTI around USD 86.4. The US administration is expected to provide details on Monday about how it intends to further isolate Iran’s economy, with traders concerned that tougher measures could trigger significant blowback from China, a key trading partner and buyer of Iranian oil. With the Middle East crisis showing few signs of easing, the risk of further disruption to regional energy flows continues to support crude and refined product prices.
#Gold: Thursday’s setback, triggered partly by rising oil prices and renewed inflation concerns, proved temporary, with gold surging again as long-end Treasury yields climbed following a Bessent interview that failed to quell investor concerns about spiralling US debt and fiscal sustainability. The ability of gold to rally alongside higher nominal yields highlights the growing importance of fiscal and debt concerns as a driver of hard-asset demand. Gold is on track for a third consecutive weekly gain and could potentially secure a weekly close above its 200-day moving average, currently near USD 4,514, strengthening the technical recovery following its recent correction.
#Copper: The transition metal trades softer on the week as LME inventories head for their biggest weekly inflow since 2020, with traders delivering metal to profit from the recent supply squeeze. Despite the immediate relief, nearby spreads remain elevated and the market vulnerable after months of inventory outflows, much of it diverted to the US ahead of a potential tariff announcement. Underlying physical supply therefore remains tight, supporting the broader bullish outlook.

The BCOM Total Return index has gained 44% over the past 12 months and 30% year-to-date, with the rally becoming increasingly broad-based as all major commodity sectors contribute. Energy and metals continue to benefit from tight supply conditions, amplified by wars, shifting trade policies and growing investor demand for hard assets amid fiscal and currency debasement concerns. Agriculture is also facing renewed upside risks, with heatwaves, increasingly volatile weather patterns and the prospect of an incoming El Niño threatening production. More in my weekly commodity update on Friday.

Meanwhile, the much hyped tech heavy Nasdaq trades up 15% YTD.

Yields rise, gold and stocks drop on renewed crude rally:
US Treasury yields have already erased yesterday’s post-buyback relief, with the 10-year rising 6 basis points to 4.70%, above the level seen before the Treasury announced its expanded buyback programme. The 30-year yield has climbed 7 basis points to 5.26%, leaving it just shy of its pre-announcement level.

The rapid reversal underlines concerns that buybacks may provide temporary liquidity support but do little to address the underlying fiscal and inflation risks driving the term premium higher. The outlook is not being helped by another increase in oil prices, with the Middle East crisis showing no signs of ending and renewed energy-price pressure adding to inflation concerns. 

Developments that are also weighing on gold following yesterday’s powerful rally, which briefly took the metal above the 200-day moving average at USD 4,511. The rebound in long-end Treasury yields, together with renewed oil-driven inflation concerns, has triggered some profit-taking and potentially forced long-liquidation from short-term focused momentum traders, all reinforcing this area as a key technical hurdle.

Chart source: Bloomberg
